question_text: A school server runs two kinds of work at the same time: short interactive requests from students using an online homework system, and long overnight-style batch jobs such as backups and report generation that are started during the day. Compare first-come first-served, round robin, priority and multilevel queue scheduling as ways of allocating CPU time on this server.
adaptation_rationale: Original question written by Claude (single-agent Chunk 3 continuation, 2026-11-04) for a syllabus statement with no linked question at handover; no historical source question or official marking status claimed.
solution: FCFS is simple with low overhead, but a long backup at the front of the queue makes every short student request wait (convoy effect), so response times are poor. Round robin gives every process a time slice in turn, so interactive requests get the CPU quickly and fairly, but frequent context switches add overhead and long batch jobs take longer to finish. Priority scheduling can give student requests a higher priority so they run first, but low-priority batch jobs may starve unless their priority is raised over time (ageing). Multilevel queue scheduling places interactive and batch processes in separate queues, each with its own algorithm (e.g. RR for interactive, FCFS for batch) and a priority between queues, so it matches this mixed workload best, although it is more complex to configure and the lower queue can still be starved. Overall, multilevel queue (or priority with ageing) suits this server better than FCFS.

marking_points.criterion: FCFS: simple/low overhead but short interactive requests wait behind long batch jobs (poor response time / convoy effect).
Round robin: time slices give fair, quick response to interactive requests.
Round robin: context-switch overhead and/or longer turnaround for long batch jobs.
Priority: interactive requests can be given precedence, but low-priority batch jobs risk starvation (ageing as mitigation).
Multilevel queue: separate queues for interactive and batch processes, each with its own algorithm and inter-queue priority.
A comparative judgement for this server (e.g. multilevel queue best fits the mixed workload, at the cost of complexity / possible starvation of the lower queue).

acceptable_alternatives: Accept a table that compares the four approaches against criteria such as response time, fairness, overhead and starvation, provided the points are linked to the scenario.
partial_credit_notes: Award each independent point once, up to 6 marks. Accept equivalent correct wording or valid alternative code. Do not double-credit one idea.
